questions.text: Do you often visit public parks or gardens in your city?

areSample.answer: Fairly regularly—I probably head to the riverside park near my flat three or four times a week.
areSample.reason: Living in a dense city, spending even twenty minutes under mature trees noticeably lowers my stress levels.
areSample.example: On warm evenings I often grab a bench by the lotus pond just to watch families walking their dogs and kids learning to cycle.

questions.text: What do people in your neighbourhood usually do when they go to the park?

areSample.answer: It really changes with the time of day, from energetic fitness groups at dawn to relaxed socialising at dusk.
areSample.reason: Because indoor gyms and large back gardens are rare in urban areas, public parks act as everyone's shared living room.
areSample.example: If you visit at six in the morning, you'll see retirees practising tai chi right beside university students running intervals.

questions.text: Did you spend much time in parks when you were growing up?

areSample.answer: Yes, practically every weekend afternoon when I was in primary school.
areSample.reason: My parents worked long hours during the week, so taking my brother and me to the local park was our favourite free outing.
areSample.example: I still vividly remember scraping my knee on the gravel path the day my father finally took the stabilisers off my bicycle.

questions.text: Do you think there are enough green spaces where you currently live?

areSample.answer: Not quite enough, especially in the rapidly expanding outer districts where new tower blocks are going up.
areSample.reason: Commercial development still tends to win out over parkland, leaving many residents a long bus ride away from decent greenery.
areSample.example: Even turning small empty corner plots into shaded pocket gardens with benches would make neighbourhood walks far more inviting.

questions.text: Would you say you have a good memory in general?

areSample.answer: I'd say my memory is quite selective—I'm great with faces, stories, and big concepts, yet hopeless with names and exact dates.
areSample.reason: My brain seems to store information far better when it's attached to a visual cue or a meaningful context.
areSample.example: I might bump into an old classmate and recall the exact joke he told ten years ago, while completely blanking on his surname.

questions.text: What techniques do you use to remember important tasks or appointments?

areSample.answer: I don't trust my unaided memory for logistics at all, so I put every appointment straight into my calendar with a reminder.
areSample.reason: Offloading routine deadlines onto a reliable system frees up mental bandwidth for creative thinking.
areSample.example: Each morning I also jot down my top three priorities on a small sticky note beside my monitor so nothing slips through the cracks.

questions.text: Are there certain things that you find unusually difficult to remember?

areSample.answer: Definitely birthdays and small household errands like buying batteries or posting a parcel.
areSample.reason: They sit outside my fixed weekly rhythm, so if I don't set an alert the moment I think of them, they vanish completely.
areSample.example: Twice this year I've walked straight past a pharmacy on my way home only to realise at my front door that I forgot to pick up plasters.

questions.text: Do you think relying on smartphones has weakened people's memories?

areSample.answer: In narrow areas like memorising phone numbers or street routes, certainly yes, though I'm not convinced our overall memory is worse.
areSample.reason: Humans have always outsourced recall to notebooks and calendars; smartphones simply accelerate that habit.
areSample.example: I couldn't recite my own sister's mobile number off the top of my head, yet I probably retain far more technical knowledge than I did a decade ago.

questions.text: Is it easy for you to stay focused on one task for a long time?

areSample.answer: It depends hugely on whether I've cleared distractions beforehand, though I can usually stay absorbed for about fifty minutes at a stretch.
areSample.reason: Even a silent notification lighting up on the desk pulls my eyes away and shatters momentum.
areSample.example: When I'm revising English essays, I put my phone in another room and work in focused fifty-minute bursts with a short walk in between.

questions.text: What tends to distract you the most when you are trying to work or study?

areSample.answer: Overhearing snippets of nearby conversation distracts me far more than steady traffic noise or rain.
areSample.reason: Human speech automatically hijacks the language centres of the brain, so I find myself eavesdropping even when I don't mean to.
areSample.example: In open-plan offices, wearing noise-cancelling headphones with gentle brown noise is the only way I can draft anything coherent.

questions.text: When during the day is it hardest for you to concentrate?

areSample.answer: Almost always between two and three in the afternoon, right after lunch.
areSample.reason: My alertness dips naturally at that hour, so attempting dense analytical reading usually means re-reading the same paragraph three times.
areSample.example: Instead of fighting it, I schedule lighter tasks like clearing emails or organising notes for that slot and take a brisk ten-minute walk.

questions.text: What helps you regain your focus when your mind starts to wander?

areSample.answer: Stepping physically away from my desk for five minutes works far better than trying to force myself to keep staring at the screen.
areSample.reason: A quick change of posture and scenery resets my attention, and shrinking the next step removes the urge to procrastinate.
areSample.example: I'll usually splash cold water on my face, make a mug of green tea, and tell myself to write just one rough paragraph when I sit back down.

questions.text: Do you enjoy going shopping in your free time?

areSample.answer: I'm not a big fan of wandering round crowded shopping centres, though I do love browsing independent bookshops and fresh food markets.
areSample.reason: For clothes or household goods, I prefer knowing exactly what I need so the trip feels brisk rather than exhausting.
areSample.example: On Sunday mornings, however, I'll happily spend an hour chatting with vendors at our neighbourhood produce market.

questions.text: Do you prefer shopping online or in physical shops?

areSample.answer: I split my habits pretty evenly: online for everyday essentials and electronics, and in-store for clothing or footwear.
areSample.reason: Comparing specifications and reading reviews is effortless online, yet nothing replaces actually feeling fabric quality or checking a shoe's fit.
areSample.example: I learnt that the hard way last year after ordering a jacket online that looked sleek in photos but turned out to be stiff and oversized.

questions.text: Are you careful about comparing prices before you buy something?

areSample.answer: For major purchases, definitely—I'll usually compare three or four retailers and wait a couple of days before checking out.
areSample.reason: That brief cooling-off period stops impulse buys and helps me judge durability rather than chasing the lowest sticker price.
areSample.example: When I bought a new desk chair recently, spending an extra twenty percent on a model with proper warranty saved me replacing a flimsy one a year later.

questions.text: Have small local shops changed much in your area in recent years?

areSample.answer: Yes, many traditional family-run corner shops have either modernised with QR payments or given way to 24-hour convenience chains.
areSample.reason: Younger shoppers expect air conditioning, clear price tags, and instant cashless checkout even for tiny errands.
areSample.example: Even the tiny stationery stall near my old school now accepts bank transfers and takes orders through a messaging app.

questions.text: Which languages can you speak, and how did you learn them?

areSample.answer: I speak Vietnamese natively and English fluently, with a smattering of basic Japanese from an elective course at university.
areSample.reason: Although school gave me a foundation in English grammar, real fluency only came once I started reading articles and listening to podcasts daily.
areSample.example: Switching my phone interface and work documentation completely into English forced me to think in the language rather than translating word for word.

questions.text: What do you find most challenging about learning a foreign language?

areSample.answer: Moving past textbook correctness to sound genuinely natural—especially mastering collocations and subtle register.
areSample.reason: You can memorise grammar rules fairly quickly, yet knowing which adjective pairs naturally with a noun only comes through massive exposure.
areSample.example: In English, for instance, it took me ages to stop translating Vietnamese phrases literally and start saying 'heavy rain' instead of 'big rain'.

questions.text: Would you like to learn another language in the future?

areSample.answer: Once I've pushed my English to a really polished level, I'd love to pick up Spanish.
areSample.reason: Its spelling is wonderfully phonetic, and speaking it would open up both travel across Latin America and a huge wealth of cinema and literature.
areSample.example: Even learning enough to chat comfortably with café owners or read street signs transforms how connected you feel on holiday.

questions.text: Do you think it is better to learn a language in a classroom or through daily practice on your own?

areSample.answer: I'd say a classroom is invaluable at the beginner stage, while independent daily habits carry you from intermediate to advanced.
areSample.reason: A good teacher catches pronunciation habits early, whereas no two-hour weekly class can match thirty minutes of focused immersion every day.
areSample.example: Using spaced-repetition flashcards and shadowing podcasts on my own has boosted my speaking fluency far faster than lectures ever did.

questions.text: Did you enjoy science lessons when you were at school?

areSample.answer: I enjoyed them enormously whenever we got into the lab, though memorising long lists of chemical equations felt a bit dry.
areSample.reason: Seeing a principle play out in front of your eyes makes abstract theory click immediately.
areSample.example: I still remember examining onion cells under a microscope in Year Eight—it made biology feel suddenly tangible rather than just diagrams on paper.

questions.text: Which branch of science interests you most nowadays?

areSample.answer: Lately I've become fascinated by cognitive science—specifically how memory, attention, and sleep interact.
areSample.reason: Unlike distant astrophysics, insights from brain research can be applied directly to how I study, rest, and manage my focus.
areSample.example: Reading about how spacing out review sessions strengthens recall completely reshaped the way I prepare for exams.

questions.text: How do you usually keep up with scientific discoveries or news?

areSample.answer: Mostly through well-researched podcasts and accessible popular-science magazines rather than short social-media posts.
areSample.reason: Brief headlines often exaggerate preliminary findings, whereas longer pieces explain the method and limitations properly.
areSample.example: Last week I listened to a brilliant forty-minute episode explaining how solid-state batteries could reshape electric transport over the next decade.

questions.text: Do you think science museums are worth visiting for adults as well as children?

areSample.answer: Without question—well-designed science museums spark just as much wonder in adults as they do in kids.
areSample.reason: Interactive displays let you test optical illusions or engineering mechanisms physically, which is far more engaging than reading static plaques.
areSample.example: When I visited a science centre abroad a couple of years ago, my friends and I spent half an hour completely absorbed by a simple wind-tunnel exhibit.

questions.text: Do you enjoy visiting art galleries or exhibitions?

areSample.answer: Yes, I really enjoy popping into a small gallery every couple of months, especially for photography or contemporary design shows.
areSample.reason: Walking through a quiet exhibition space forces you to slow down and notice textures, light, and composition without any rush.
areSample.example: Last month I visited a local lacquer-painting exhibition and was amazed by how many months of layering go into a single panel.

questions.text: Did you enjoy drawing or painting when you were a child?

areSample.answer: I loved it—I used to fill the back pages of all my school exercise books with pencil sketches and miniature comic strips.
areSample.reason: As a kid you don't worry about whether something looks polished; you just enjoy inventing little worlds on paper.
areSample.example: I even won a small ribbon in primary school for a watercolour poster of our local fishing harbour.

questions.text: Do you have any artwork or posters displayed in your home?

areSample.answer: Yes, I have two framed botanical prints above my desk and a small watercolour landscape I picked up at a weekend craft fair.
areSample.reason: Bare white walls make a rented flat feel rather sterile, whereas a couple of thoughtfully chosen prints immediately give a room personality.
areSample.example: Whenever I look up from my monitor, the muted green tones of those prints help my eyes relax.

questions.text: Do you think art lessons should be compulsory for all school students?

areSample.answer: I think they should definitely be compulsory through primary and lower secondary school, then optional in the final exam years.
areSample.reason: Art nurtures observation, patience, and visual thinking—skills that serve future engineers and architects just as much as painters.
areSample.example: Even students who never pursue fine arts benefit from having one weekly period where there isn't just a single right answer.

questions.text: Are you interested in learning about history?
ideaHintsEn: grew fond of it as an adult

areSample.answer: Much more so now than when I was in school, especially social history about how ordinary people lived day to day.
areSample.reason: School exams often reduced history to memorising dates of treaties, whereas reading personal letters and trade histories brings an era alive.
areSample.example: I recently watched a fascinating documentary on ancient maritime spice routes that completely changed how I look at coastal towns in Asia.

questions.text: Do you like visiting historical sites or heritage buildings?

areSample.answer: Very much—standing inside a centuries-old courtyard gives you a sense of scale that no textbook photograph can replicate.
areSample.reason: Seeing worn stone steps and traditional carpentry makes the past feel genuinely human rather than abstract.
areSample.example: When I visited the imperial citadel in Hue last year, hiring a local guide turned what could have been simple ruins into vivid stories.

questions.text: How did you mainly learn about history when you were younger?

areSample.answer: Formally through school textbooks, of course, yet the stories that actually stuck with me came from my grandfather.
areSample.reason: Hearing first-hand anecdotes about rationing, old bicycles, and neighbourhood life carried an emotional weight no worksheet could match.
areSample.example: I still remember him describing how the whole street used to gather round a single black-and-white television set in the evening.

questions.text: Do you think historical films are a good way for people to learn about the past?

areSample.answer: They're a brilliant gateway for sparking curiosity, provided viewers remember that filmmakers compress timelines for dramatic effect.
areSample.reason: Strong costumes, dialect, and atmosphere draw in audiences who might never pick up a five-hundred-page academic biography.
areSample.example: Whenever a well-crafted period drama catches my interest, I usually end up reading a couple of proper historical essays afterwards to separate fact from fiction.

questions.text: How many hours of sleep do you usually get on a typical night?
ideaHintsEn: around seven to seven and a half hours

areSample.answer: I aim for roughly seven and a half hours most nights, going to bed around eleven and waking up at half past six.
areSample.reason: I've learnt the hard way that cutting sleep down to five or six hours might feel productive on the night, yet wrecks my judgement the next day.
areSample.example: Whenever I stick to a steady bedtime all week, I barely even need an alarm clock by Friday morning.

questions.text: Do you ever take a nap during the daytime?

areSample.answer: Yes, a brief twenty-minute power nap after lunch is fairly common here, and I swear by it when I'm working from home.
areSample.reason: Keeping it under twenty-five minutes refreshes my memory without letting me drop into deep sleep, which would leave me groggy.
areSample.example: I just set a quiet timer on my desk, close the blinds for fifteen minutes, and wake up feeling ready for the afternoon.

questions.text: What helps you fall asleep easily at night?

areSample.answer: Keeping the bedroom cool, avoiding caffeine after two in the afternoon, and reading a few pages of fiction before lights out.
areSample.reason: That predictable wind-down sequence acts as a signal to my nervous system that the workday is genuinely over.
areSample.example: On nights when my mind is still racing about a deadline, jotting tomorrow's to-do list on a notepad next to my bed clears my head almost immediately.

questions.text: Do you think people today get less sleep than people did in the past?

areSample.answer: Almost certainly yes, largely because glowing screens and round-the-clock entertainment have pushed bedtimes later and later.
areSample.reason: Decades ago, darkness and limited broadcast hours naturally nudged households to turn in early, whereas now there's always one more episode or message.
areSample.example: Many of my colleagues openly joke about 'revenge bedtime procrastination'—staying up past midnight simply to reclaim quiet personal time.

questions.text: Are you generally good at managing your time?

areSample.answer: I'm reasonably disciplined nowadays, though it took a few stressful university deadlines to teach me proper planning.
areSample.reason: Breaking large projects into concrete half-hour blocks stops me from staring at a vague goal and putting it off.
areSample.example: Every Sunday evening I spend ten minutes mapping out my main work blocks and study sessions for the week ahead.

questions.text: How do you feel when you are kept waiting by someone who is late?

areSample.answer: If they send a quick heads-up, I don't mind waiting ten or fifteen minutes at all, though being left guessing does irritate me.
areSample.reason: Traffic and unforeseen delays happen to everyone; it's the lack of courtesy rather than the delay itself that stings.
areSample.example: Usually I just pull out my e-reader or review vocabulary flashcards so the spare quarter of an hour doesn't feel wasted.

questions.text: What usually makes it hardest for you to stick to a schedule?

areSample.answer: Underestimating how long fiddly tasks actually take, especially when I forget to leave buffer time between commitments.
areSample.reason: When a calendar is packed back to back, a single ten-minute overrun creates a domino effect across the whole afternoon.
areSample.example: I've recently started adding a twenty-percent cushion to my estimates, which has made my days far calmer.

questions.text: Do you prefer planning every detail of your day or keeping things flexible?

areSample.answer: I prefer structuring my core priorities while leaving room to shift things around if unexpected opportunities pop up.
areSample.reason: Minute-by-minute timetables feel suffocating and collapse the instant real life interferes.
areSample.example: As long as I finish my two non-negotiable tasks before lunch, I'm happy to keep the late afternoon fairly fluid.

questions.text: Do you enjoy choosing gifts for other people?
ideaHintsEn: can feel tricky for picky people

areSample.answer: I really do, provided I know the person well enough to pick something genuinely thoughtful rather than a generic voucher.
areSample.reason: Seeing someone light up because you remembered a passing remark they made months earlier is wonderfully rewarding.
areSample.example: I keep a private note on my phone where I jot down books or gadgets friends mention wanting throughout the year.

questions.text: What kind of gifts do you usually prefer to receive?

areSample.answer: I'm happiest with practical things I'll actually use or consumables like good coffee beans, tea, or a hand-picked book.
areSample.reason: Living in a compact flat, I try to avoid decorative clutter, whereas something consumable or experiential brings joy without taking up shelf space.
areSample.example: Last birthday a friend gave me a bag of single-origin roast from Da Lat and a handwritten card, and I enjoyed every single cup.

questions.text: On what occasions do people in your country normally exchange gifts?
ideaHintsEn: Lunar New Year hampers and lucky money

areSample.answer: Lunar New Year is by far the biggest occasion, alongside weddings, housewarmings, and Teachers' Day in November.
areSample.reason: Gift-giving here is strongly tied to expressing gratitude and strengthening family or community bonds rather than just celebrating birthdays.
areSample.example: During Tet, it's customary to bring gift baskets of tea, dried fruit, and traditional cakes when visiting older relatives.

questions.text: Do you think an expensive gift is always better than a handmade or modest one?

areSample.answer: Not at all—in fact, overly lavish gifts can sometimes make the recipient feel uncomfortable or indebted.
areSample.reason: What makes a present memorable is the time and personal observation behind it, not the receipt.
areSample.example: One of my most treasured possessions is simply a ceramic mug my sister painted at a pottery workshop for my graduation.

questions.text: Do you use maps very often in your daily life?

areSample.answer: Almost every couple of days—not only to find unfamiliar addresses, but also to check live traffic bottlenecks before setting off.
areSample.reason: In a dense city with narrow alleys, even a small road closure can double your journey time if you don't glance at a route map first.
areSample.example: Yesterday evening checking my map app spotted a flooded junction early and saved me at least twenty minutes on the way to dinner.

questions.text: Do you prefer digital navigation apps or traditional paper maps?

areSample.answer: Digital maps win hands down for everyday navigation, though I still have a soft spot for paper maps when planning a scenic trip.
areSample.reason: Unfolding a large printed map lets you grasp the entire geography of a region at once, whereas a small phone screen encourages tunnel vision.
areSample.example: On a national park hike last year, I carried a printed trail map as a backup because mobile signal vanished completely in the valley.

questions.text: Would you say you have a good sense of direction?

areSample.answer: Outdoors in daylight, yes—I usually orient myself quickly using rivers, tall landmarks, and the position of the sun.
areSample.reason: Once I've walked a neighbourhood twice without staring at a blue dot, a mental map starts to lock in naturally.
areSample.example: Put me inside a massive underground shopping mall with identical exits, though, and I can lose my bearings in thirty seconds.

questions.text: Do you think children should still be taught how to read paper maps at school?

areSample.answer: Yes, definitely—not because they'll abandon GPS, but because reading maps builds vital spatial reasoning.
areSample.reason: Understanding scale, contour lines, and compass directions trains kids to think geographically rather than blindly following voice prompts.
areSample.example: It's also a practical safety skill on school camping trips whenever batteries run flat or signal drops out.

questions.text: Do you have a favourite colour?

areSample.answer: I've always been drawn to muted forest green and deep navy blue.
areSample.reason: Both shades feel calm and grounded without being dull, and they pair effortlessly with neutral tones in clothing or interiors.
areSample.example: If you glanced at my desk right now, you'd see a dark green notebook, a navy laptop sleeve, and a sage-coloured ceramic mug.

questions.text: Do certain colours have special meanings in your culture?

areSample.answer: Very much so—red and bright yellow are strongly linked with good fortune, celebration, and renewal.
areSample.reason: Those traditional associations still guide how families decorate their homes and dress for major milestones.
areSample.example: During Lunar New Year, streets fill with red lucky-money envelopes and golden apricot blossoms, whereas plain white is traditionally reserved for funerals.

questions.text: Does the colour of a room affect how you feel inside it?

areSample.answer: Surprisingly strongly—soft, warm neutrals and earthy accents help me unwind, whereas stark fluorescent white feels clinical.
areSample.reason: Wall colour interacts closely with lighting, subtly shaping whether a room feels spacious and peaceful or tense.
areSample.example: When I painted my study corner a pale warm grey instead of bright hospital white, working late immediately felt far easier on my eyes.

questions.text: Do you pay much attention to colour when buying clothes?

areSample.answer: Quite a bit, because sticking to a cohesive palette makes getting dressed in the morning effortless.
areSample.reason: If most of my shirts and trousers sit in navy, charcoal, olive, and off-white, practically everything matches without much thought.
areSample.example: Every now and then I'll throw in a burgundy scarf or mustard tote bag just to stop the outfit looking too monochrome.

questions.text: How do you usually spend your weekends?

areSample.answer: I tend to split my weekend neatly: Saturday is for socialising and getting out, while Sunday is reserved for quiet recharging.
areSample.reason: Having one lively day and one unhurried day stops me from arriving at Monday morning feeling like I need another holiday.
areSample.example: Usually I'll meet friends for coffee or badminton on Saturday, then spend Sunday cooking, reading, and tidying my flat.

questions.text: Do you usually plan your weekend activities in advance?

areSample.answer: I like to lock in just one main anchor—say, dinner with friends or a morning hike—and leave the rest completely spontaneous.
areSample.reason: Planning every single hour turns leisure time into another rigid schedule.
areSample.example: Last Saturday, having a free afternoon meant I could spontaneously drop into a street book fair I spotted on my walk home.

questions.text: Which day of the weekend do you enjoy more, Saturday or Sunday?

areSample.answer: Definitely Saturday, especially Saturday morning when the whole weekend still stretches ahead.
areSample.reason: By late Sunday afternoon, a faint sense of Monday preparation always starts creeping into the back of my mind.
areSample.example: Sitting on my balcony with a slow pour-over coffee at eight on a Saturday feels like pure luxury.

questions.text: Do you ever have to work or study at the weekend?

areSample.answer: I guard my weekends tightly against office work, though I do put in an hour or two of self-paced English study.
areSample.reason: Studying something I've chosen for my own long-term goals feels energising rather than draining, unlike answering work emails.
areSample.example: Typically I'll do one timed reading practice on Sunday morning and then close the laptop for the rest of the day.

questions.text: What are your main goals for the next year or two?

areSample.answer: My top priority over the next twelve months is achieving a strong IELTS Academic score while deepening my technical leadership skills at work.
areSample.reason: Having a solid English qualification keeps international study and career doors wide open without forcing a rushed decision.
areSample.example: I've set up a consistent forty-five-minute daily study routine so progress builds steadily rather than relying on last-minute cramming.

questions.text: Would you like to live or work abroad at some point in the future?

areSample.answer: Yes, I'd love to spend two or three years studying or working abroad, perhaps in the UK, Australia, or Northern Europe.
areSample.reason: Immersing yourself in a different workplace culture stretches your independence and exposes you to new ways of tackling problems.
areSample.example: In the long run I can still picture returning home, bringing back both international experience and a wider professional network.

questions.text: Is there a practical skill you hope to master in the coming years?

areSample.answer: I'm determined to become a much more confident public speaker, especially when presenting complex ideas to non-technical audiences.
areSample.reason: Strong analytical work often goes unnoticed unless you can explain it clearly, concisely, and persuasively in front of a room.
areSample.example: I've started volunteering to host short ten-minute demos at work so I get regular practice speaking under gentle pressure.

questions.text: Do you think it is better to set detailed long-term plans or take life one step at a time?

areSample.answer: I favour having a clear sense of direction rather than a rigid five-year blueprint.
areSample.reason: Industries and personal priorities shift so quickly nowadays that clinging stubbornly to an outdated plan can blind you to better paths.
areSample.example: For me, setting concrete goals twelve months ahead while keeping a loose compass for the next five years strikes the healthiest balance.
